$comment: Endnotes for EVERY FLAT MAP IS A CHOICE (home.md §14). Grouped by chapter; each entry carries a citation, an external link, and an optional editorial note. Consumed by the on-page sources list in Ch14Colophon.tsx (the SourcesDrawerProvider drawer opened from nav/footnotes mirrors the same citations). Chapter anchors deep-link into the essay.

entries.citation: Snyder, J. P. (1987). Map Projections: A Working Manual. USGS Professional Paper 1395. United States Government Printing Office, Washington.
entries.note: The working manual behind our distortion math: Tissot's indicatrix and the scale-factor derivations (equations 4-1 to 4-12).

entries.citation: Goldberg, D. M., & Gott, J. R. (2007). “Flexion and Skewness in Map Projections of the Earth.” Cartographica 42(4), 297–318.
entries.note: The flexion/skewness decomposition referenced when the scorecard separates kinds of distortion.

entries.citation: PROJ documentation — Mercator (merc) projection reference page.
entries.note: Forward/inverse formulas and the standard ±85° truncation used by web maps.

entries.citation: PROJ documentation — Cylindrical Equal Area (cea) projection reference page.
entries.note: Gall–Peters is cea with standard parallels at 45°; our Peters math follows this reference.

entries.citation: Šavrič, B., Patterson, T., & Jenny, B. (2019). “The Equal Earth map projection.” International Journal of Geographical Information Science 33(3), 454–465.
entries.note: The published coefficients A₁=1.340264, A₂=−0.081106, A₃=0.000893, A₄=0.003796 with M=√3/2 are baked into src/data/equalearth.json; our reference test points match the paper and PROJ.

entries.citation: PROJ documentation — Equal Earth (eqearth) projection reference page.
entries.note: Source of the MAX_Y constant 1.3173627591574 and the Newton–Raphson inverse our Python panel demonstrates.

entries.citation: Kerkovits, K. (2021). “Image-Based Angular Distortion Metric for Comparing World Map Projections.” ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information 11(1):1.
entries.note: Published angular RMSE 2.678° for Equal Earth, quoted as a reference anchor in the scorecard.

entries.citation: Narukawa, H. (2022). “Formulation of AuthaGraph Map Projection and an Evaluation of its Distortion.” Map (Journal of the Japan Cartographers Association) 60(1), 1–16. J-STAGE.
entries.note: Our implementation uses Narukawa's published 2022 formulation (four cones approximating the original hand-built curved tetrahedron, <4% radial deviation); area is exact at the 96-region level, multi-objective in intent — not infinitesimally equal-area.

entries.citation: González, Á. (2010). “Measurement of Areas on a Sphere Using Fibonacci and Latitude–Longitude Lattices.” Mathematical Geosciences 42, 49–64.
entries.note: The 5,001-point Fibonacci sampling scheme behind our measured RMS log-area and angular-distortion scores.

entries.citation: Natural Earth — physical vectors (land, lakes, coastline), public domain. Data is bundled with this site.
entries.note: The main globe and maps use 1:50 million land, lake and coastline data. Legacy demonstrations and region comparisons also use the bundled 1:110 million and curated boundary datasets.

entries.citation: NASA Blue Marble Next Generation — July 2004, with topography and bathymetry. 5,400 × 2,700 pixel global composite.
entries.note: NASA Earth Observatory. The globe uses this cloud-free composite for land cover, ice and ocean detail; it is not live satellite imagery.

entries.citation: UN News, September 4, 2026 — reporting on the decision to encourage equal-area projections for general-reference world maps.
entries.note: The cartographic tradeoff: equal-area maps preserve relative sizes; Mercator preserves local angles and supports constant-bearing navigation.

entries.citation: United Nations Group of Experts on Geographical Names (UNGEGN) — standardization of geographical names.
entries.note: Names on this site (e.g. “Gulf of Mexico”, “Lake Ontario”) follow the UNGEGN standardization process and are baked into a curated static dataset (src/data/labels.json) at build time.

entries.citation: International Hydrographic Organization — publication S-23, “Limits of Oceans and Seas”, for marine feature names and extents.
entries.note: Ocean naming (the five oceans shown on the closing globe) follows IHO usage.
